paragraphs: Psychology is the scientific study of how minds work and why people think, feel and act as they do. Claims about people are hard to test, because people vary, forget things, guess what a study is about and see patterns that are not there. Learning how the field copes with that is the best way to judge what it says about sleep, memory or why a crowd stands by while someone needs help.

The course has twelve lessons in four parts. The first part, How we know, covers what a correlation can and cannot show, why random assignment makes a fair comparison, and how to tell a big effect from a lucky one. Perception and attention looks at detecting faint signals, at what attention hides, and at how the mind combines cues. Memory and learning covers holding things in mind, forgetting and spaced retrieval, and conditioning. Thinking and the social mind finishes with base rates, anchors and fast intuition, and conformity, obedience and bystanders.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, and most put numbers on an idea so that you can check the result yourself.
outcomes: You'll be able to say why a correlation does not show a cause and name other explanations for it.
You'll be able to judge how big a research finding is and how many people a study needs to find it.
You'll be able to separate how well someone detects a faint signal from how readily they say yes.
You'll be able to work out how likely a positive result is to be right once the base rate is counted.
You'll be able to explain how forgetting, conditioning and the pull of a crowd shape what people remember and do.
prerequisites: You should be comfortable with percentages, square roots and simple algebra, and you need no earlier psychology or statistics.
